title: Type coercion errors
story:
Somewhere between the source and your code, something looks at a value written as text and decides what kind of thing it is. That guess is made per value, from its appearance, and the appearance of a value is not the same as its meaning.

The best-documented case in the literature is a spreadsheet turning gene names into dates. On default settings the program converts certain gene symbols into dates and into floating point numbers, and the behaviour was first characterised in 2004 by Zeeberg and colleagues. In 2016 a programmatic scan of supplementary files from eighteen genomics journals published between 2005 and 2015 found that roughly one fifth of papers carrying supplementary gene lists contained these conversions — and, of the 987 affected files, 166 held no accession numbers or genomic coordinates from which the original names could be recovered. The information was not damaged. It was gone.

What happened next is the part worth sitting with. A follow-up scan covering 2014 to 2020 assembled 166,139 articles, found 11,117 with gene symbol lists, and confirmed errors in 3,436 of them: 30.9 percent, against the 19.6 percent reported earlier. The publicity had not helped. Errors continued to accumulate unabated in the period after 2016.

So in 2020 the nomenclature committee renamed the genes. SEPT1 became SEPTIN1; MARCH1 became MARCHF1. Human, mouse and rat symbols were updated, other species were not, and a scan of eukaryotic annotations still found 1,544 names across 104 taxa that convert to dates. Read that plainly: an international scientific body changed the names of human genes because a type inference rule in a spreadsheet would not change. That is how strong a default is, and it is the reason this lesson sits in a data track rather than in a list of quirks.

The defence is simple to state and requires discipline to apply. Read every column as text. Convert each one explicitly, having decided what it is. Never let a loader infer, because inference is re-run on every load and its answer depends on the values that happened to arrive — one file where every identifier looks numeric and one where a single value does not, and the same column comes back as two different types on two different days. The type of a column is a claim about the data, not a property of any value in it.

problem.name: Type inference on load
problem.shape: Values arrive as text and something decides what kind of thing each one is by how it is written, before your code sees it.
tell: the loader was given no schema and worked it out
a column holds identifiers, codes or symbols that resemble numbers or dates
the same column has come back with different types on different days
a value has leading zeros, or a letter that most of its neighbours lack
problem.move: Read every column as text and convert explicitly, having decided in advance what each one is. Put the declared types under version control next to the loader, and assert them on read, so that a file which does not match stops the pipeline rather than changing the meaning of a column.
problem.invariant: The type of a column is a property of the column, not of any value in it. Inference decides per value from appearance, so it can only ever be right by coincidence across a whole column.
problem.breaks: Declaring types stops your loader from guessing; it does not stop anything upstream. The conversion usually happened before the file reached you, in a tool nobody in the pipeline controls, and by then the strictest possible reader can only tell you the column is text — not what the text used to be.

cost.time: you must know what every column is before you can load it, which is the work that inference existed to avoid
cost.space: none; a schema is a few lines
cost.beats: cleaning the output, which is repair by guesswork — it produces plausible values and removes the evidence that anything was ever wrong

worked.problem: A column of identifiers has come back with some of its values converted into dates. Can you recover them?
worked.reasoning:
Sometimes, and you cannot tell which case you are in by looking at the column.

The conversion is lossy in a way that depends on the value. A symbol that becomes a date has been re-encoded into an internal serial number, and a symbol that becomes a floating point number has been re-encoded too. What made it recoverable or not is whether the original string can be inferred from the result and the surrounding context — and for a substantial fraction it cannot. In the 2016 scan, 166 of the 987 affected files held no accession numbers or genomic coordinates alongside the converted names, and for those files nothing in the file identifies what the original symbols were. Not corrupted, not garbled: absent.

Where recovery is possible it comes from redundancy, never from the damaged column. If another column identifies the same entity — an accession, a coordinate, a stable identifier — you can map back through that. If you hold the source file before the conversion, you re-read it with types declared. If a known finite vocabulary exists, you can sometimes invert the mapping, but only where it is injective; if two distinct symbols convert to the same representation, no amount of cleverness separates them afterwards.

So the honest answer in an interview is: recovery is a question about what else is in the dataset, not about the column, and the correct move is to go back to the source rather than to write a repair function. A repair function that guesses is worse than the original error, because it produces plausible values and removes the evidence that anything went wrong.

And the reason I would not treat it as an edge case: the follow-up scan found the error rate had gone up after the problem was published, from 19.6 to 30.9 percent, and the eventual response was that the nomenclature committee renamed the genes. When the remedy for a coercion bug is to rename the entities of an entire field, the lesson is not that this particular program is badly behaved. It is that type inference on load is a guess that gets re-made on every file, and the only defence is to declare the type instead.

problem.practice: Take a loader you use and check whether it infers types. Feed it two files that differ only in one value — one where every entry in a column looks numeric, one where a single entry does not — and compare the resulting types. Then write the schema down, assert it, and confirm that the second file now fails loudly instead of quietly changing the column.

beats.broke: A value arrives written as text, and something between the source and your code decides what kind of thing it is by looking at how it is written — one value at a time, from appearance rather than meaning.
beats.fix: Read everything as text and convert explicitly, column by column, because the type of a column is a fact about the column rather than a property of any value in it.
beats.cost: Explicit typing means knowing what every column is before you can load it, and it only defends your own boundary — the coercion has usually already happened upstream, in a tool nobody in the pipeline controls.

interview.q: A column of identifiers has come back with some of its values converted into dates. Can you recover them?
interview.trap: Promising a repair function. Where the conversion was not injective, or where no other column identifies the same entity, the original values are absent rather than damaged — and a repair that guesses produces plausible values while erasing the evidence that anything went wrong.
interview.answer:
Sometimes — and you cannot tell which case you are in by inspecting the column.

The conversion re-encodes the value, and whether the original can be inferred depends on what else is in the file rather than on the damaged column. In the 2016 scan, 166 of the 987 affected files carried no accession numbers or genomic coordinates alongside the converted names. For those files the original symbols are not garbled, they are absent; nothing in the file identifies what they were.

Where recovery is possible, it comes from redundancy. Another column identifying the same entity lets you map back. The source file before conversion lets you re-read with types declared. A known finite vocabulary lets you invert the mapping — but only where the mapping is injective, and if two distinct symbols converted to the same representation, nothing separates them afterwards.

So the answer I would give is that this is a question about what else the dataset contains, and the right move is to return to the source rather than write a repair function. A repair that guesses is worse than the original error, because it produces plausible values and erases the evidence that anything went wrong.

I would add why this is not an edge case. After the problem was published the rate went up, from 19.6 to 30.9 percent, and the eventual remedy was that the nomenclature committee renamed the genes — SEPT1 to SEPTIN1, MARCH1 to MARCHF1. When the fix for a coercion bug is to rename the entities of an entire scientific field, the conclusion is not that one program misbehaves. It is that inferring types at load time is a guess re-made on every file, and the defence is to declare the type instead.

   text in  ->  "what kind of thing is this?"
                decided per VALUE, by APPEARANCE

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A BUG

   inference is re-run on every load.

   file A: every id looks numeric   -> numeric
   file B: one id has a letter      -> text

   same column. same pipeline.
   two types on two days.

   987 files with converted gene names
   166 with nothing else to recover them from

   -> recovery is a question about REDUNDANCY
      elsewhere in the data, never about the
      damaged column.

   and if two distinct values converted to the
   same representation, nothing separates them
   afterwards.

THE SCOREBOARD

   2004  behaviour characterised
   2016  ~1 in 5 papers affected        19.6%
   2021  after the publicity            30.9%
   2020  the committee renamed the GENES
           SEPT1  -> SEPTIN1
           MARCH1 -> MARCHF1

THE RULE

   a column's type is a CLAIM about the data,
   not a property of any value in it.

   declare it. do not infer it.
   and go back to the source rather than
   writing a repair that guesses.
takeaway: Type inference decides per value from appearance and is re-run on every load, which is why a column can come back as two different types on two different days — and why an international committee renamed human genes rather than wait for a spreadsheet default to change.
